scenes.visual: Title card: Water, Salt and Nitrogenous Waste. Show sea, fresh water and land.

scenes.tts: Every animal must balance water and salt gains and losses. The surroundings keep pulling them the other way. A marine bony fish loses water and gains salt. In fresh water, water enters and salts leak out. On land, evaporation threatens the water supply. Even marine invertebrates whose body fluids follow the sea must adjust organic molecules inside their cells. That keeps the cells from swelling or shrinking. Nitrogen disposal also uses water.

scenes.visual: Open with the shared water and salt budget. Compare a marine bony fish losing water and gaining salt, a freshwater bony fish gaining water and losing salt, and a land animal losing water by evaporation. Use blue water arrows and yellow salt arrows with separate labels. Then show a marine invertebrate cell adjusting organic osmolytes as external concentration changes, maintaining cell volume. End with nitrogen waste linked to water loss. No numerical scales.

scenes.tts: Marine bony fish drink seawater. The intestine absorbs water and ions. Excess sodium and chloride leave mostly through the gills. Absorbed magnesium and sulfate leave through the kidneys in a small volume of urine. Freshwater bony fish face the reverse problem. Their kidneys make plenty of dilute urine. Their gills actively take up sodium and chloride, using A T P. In salmon and eels moving between these worlds, gill cells switch between salt uptake and secretion.

scenes.visual: Compare the coordinated routes in marine and freshwater teleosts. Marine: seawater to gut, water and ions absorbed; sodium and chloride out at gills; absorbed magnesium and sulfate out in a small urine stream. Freshwater: water enters and salt leaks across gills; active sodium and chloride uptake uses ATP; large dilute urine stream. Finish with salmon or eel gill transport switching direction. Avoid implying that all ingested magnesium and sulfate are absorbed.

scenes.tts: Protein breakdown produces ammonia. It needs no A T P to form, but it is toxic and takes plenty of water to excrete. Urea costs A T P to make. It is less toxic and needs less water. Uric acid leaves as a paste or solid with very little water. It is usually costlier still to make. Each waste trades toxicity, water and energy.

scenes.visual: Show protein breakdown leading to ammonia, then compare ammonia, urea and uric acid in a qualitative table: toxicity, water needed and synthesis cost. Mark ammonia as no ATP to form, urea as ATP required, and uric acid as usually costlier still with minimal water loss. Show dissolved wastes versus uric acid paste. Do not add numerical values or a fixed habitat hierarchy.

scenes.tts: Organs control what leaves. Most vertebrate kidneys filter body fluid, then reabsorb useful substances and secrete others into the tubule. Insect Malpighian tubules do not filter. They secrete ions into the tubule, and water follows by osmosis. Wastes enter too. The rectum then recovers salts and water.

scenes.visual: Define filtration, reabsorption and secretion with labeled arrows. Contrast a vertebrate kidney filtering at the glomerulus and modifying filtrate with an insect Malpighian tubule secreting ions and wastes into its lumen. Show water following ions by osmosis, then water and salt recovery at the rectum. Label the kidney pattern as most vertebrate kidneys.

scenes.tts: Sharks retain urea for another purpose: water balance. Urea and other dissolved particles bring their blood slightly above seawater in total concentration, so water enters slowly. Their kidneys recover most filtered urea. They still regulate salts. A rectal gland secretes concentrated sodium chloride.

scenes.visual: Show shark plasma with separate contributions from inorganic ions, retained urea and TMAO, without numerical values. Label total osmolality slightly above seawater and show slow water entry. Show kidneys returning filtered urea to blood and the rectal gland secreting sodium chloride. Keep salt concentration distinct from total osmolality.

scenes.tts: One smaller example: seabirds use nasal salt glands. Salt secretion more concentrated than seawater lets them clear a gulp of seawater's salt in less water than the gulp held. They keep the difference.
